metadata.notes: Four-phase plan: Observe → Expose → Scale → Tune. Each phase delivers standalone value. Phase 1 is useful even without auto-scaling (operational visibility). Phase 2 lights up the dashboard. Phase 3 is the core feature. Phase 4 is refinement. Batch refs W01-W20.

issues.title: Implement system metrics collector (CPU, memory, goroutines)

sections.summary: Create internal/metrics/system.go that periodically collects system-level resource metrics using Go's runtime package and /proc filesystem.
sections.context:
Go's runtime package provides: runtime.NumGoroutine(), runtime.ReadMemStats() for heap/stack/GC stats, and runtime.NumCPU(). For CPU utilization, read /proc/stat (Linux) or use a lightweight poller — the gopsutil library is an option but adds a dependency. Since CT 202 is an LXC container on Proxmox, /proc reflects the container's view (cgroup-limited resources), which is exactly what we want.

Collect at a configurable interval (default: 10 seconds). Store as a rolling window in memory (last N samples, default: 360 = 1 hour at 10s intervals). No external dependencies — this runs inside the samverk binary.

Design the collector as an interface so it's testable:

```go
type SystemMetrics struct {
    Timestamp      time.Time
    CPUPercent     float64   // 0-100 per core, or total
    MemoryUsedMB   float64
    MemoryTotalMB  float64
    MemoryPercent  float64   // 0-100
    HeapAllocMB    float64   // Go heap
    HeapSysMB      float64   // Go heap reserved from OS
    GoroutineCount int
    NumGC          uint32    // GC cycles since start
}

type Collector interface {
    Start(ctx context.Context)
    Latest() *SystemMetrics
    History(duration time.Duration) []SystemMetrics
    Stop()
}
```

The collector should be started alongside the dispatcher and agent pool in cmd/samverk/main.go.
acceptance_criteria: internal/metrics/system.go implements Collector interface
Collects CPU percent, memory used/total/percent, Go heap stats, goroutine count, GC count
Rolling window stores configurable number of samples in memory
CPU measurement uses /proc/stat delta between samples (not instantaneous)
Collector is safe for concurrent reads from API handlers
Unit tests with mock /proc data or runtime.MemStats injection
go test -race ./internal/metrics/... passes

issues.title: Implement agent pool metrics (active workers, queue depth, task durations)

sections.summary: Add instrumentation to the agent pool to track operational metrics: active workers, idle workers, queue depth, task execution times, and provider response times.
sections.context:
The current Pool struct in internal/agent/pool.go has no observability. Add metrics tracking without changing the pool's external API. Key metrics:

```go
type PoolMetrics struct {
    Timestamp        time.Time
    TotalWorkers     int       // configured worker count
    ActiveWorkers    int       // currently executing a task
    IdleWorkers      int       // waiting on channel
    QueueDepth       int       // len(p.tasks)
    QueueCapacity    int       // cap(p.tasks)
    TasksCompleted   int64     // lifetime counter
    TasksFailed      int64     // lifetime counter
    AvgTaskDuration  time.Duration  // rolling average
    LastTaskDuration time.Duration
    ProviderLatency  map[string]time.Duration  // per-provider average response time
}
```

Active vs idle tracking: increment an atomic counter when processTask starts, decrement when it returns. Queue depth is just len(p.tasks). Task duration is measured around the runner.Run() call. Provider latency comes from the runner's provider call timing.

Expose via a method: `pool.Metrics() *PoolMetrics`

This is the pool's side of the observability story — W01 handles the system side.
acceptance_criteria: Pool tracks active/idle worker counts via atomic counters
Queue depth and capacity exposed
Task completion and failure counters (lifetime, atomic int64)
Rolling average task duration calculated over last N tasks (default: 50)
Per-provider latency tracking (average over last N calls)
pool.Metrics() returns a snapshot safe for concurrent access
No performance regression — all tracking uses atomics or minimal locking
Unit tests verify counter increments and duration tracking
go test -race ./internal/agent/... passes

issues.title: Add /api/v1/metrics endpoint combining system, pool, and dispatcher metrics

sections.summary: Add a REST endpoint that returns a combined metrics snapshot: system resources, pool state, and dispatcher state. Also update /healthz to include resource pressure indicators.
sections.context:
Add to internal/api/api.go:

```go
// GET /api/v1/metrics
type MetricsResponse struct {
    System     *metrics.SystemMetrics     `json:"system"`
    Pool       *agent.PoolMetrics         `json:"pool"`
    Dispatcher *dispatcher.DispatcherMetrics `json:"dispatcher"`
    Pressure   PressureIndicator          `json:"pressure"`
}

type PressureIndicator struct {
    Level   string  `json:"level"`   // "low", "moderate", "high", "critical"
    Reasons []string `json:"reasons"` // ["CPU above 80%", "All workers busy"]
}
```

Pressure levels are simple threshold checks for Phase 2:
- low: CPU < 50%, memory < 60%, idle workers > 0
- moderate: CPU 50-80% OR memory 60-80% OR queue depth > 0
- high: CPU > 80% OR memory > 80% OR all workers busy with queued tasks
- critical: CPU > 95% OR memory > 90%

These thresholds are configuration-driven for Phase 3 tuning. Also add /api/v1/metrics/history?duration=1h for time-series data from the rolling window.

Update /healthz to include pressure level (existing clients still get {status: ok} but with an additional pressure field).
acceptance_criteria: GET /api/v1/metrics returns combined system, pool, and dispatcher metrics
Pressure indicator calculated from current metrics with threshold logic
GET /api/v1/metrics/history returns time-series data for the requested duration
/healthz response includes pressure level without breaking existing consumers
Endpoints require API key auth (same as existing API endpoints)
Unit tests for pressure calculation logic

issues.title: Refactor agent pool to support dynamic worker add/remove

sections.summary: Refactor the agent Pool to support adding and removing workers at runtime while maintaining the existing Submit/Shutdown contract.
sections.context:
The current Pool in internal/agent/pool.go spawns a fixed number of goroutines in NewPool and the only termination path is Shutdown() which closes the task channel. Dynamic scaling requires:

1. **Adding workers:** Straightforward — start a new goroutine reading from p.tasks, increment p.wg counter. But wg.Add must happen before the goroutine starts, and the goroutine must call wg.Done on exit.

2. **Removing workers:** Harder — you can't selectively stop one goroutine reading from a shared channel. Options:
   a. Per-worker quit channel: each worker has its own `quit chan struct{}`. To remove a worker, close its quit channel. Worker selects on both `p.tasks` and `quit`.
   b. Sentinel task: send a special 'stop' task that causes the receiving worker to exit.
   c. Context-based: each worker gets a cancellable context.

   Option (a) is cleanest — each worker is independently addressable.

3. **Pool resize method:**
```go
func (p *Pool) Resize(target int) error  // set desired worker count
func (p *Pool) ScaleUp(n int) error      // add n workers
func (p *Pool) ScaleDown(n int) error    // remove n workers (graceful drain)
func (p *Pool) WorkerCount() int         // current count
```

ScaleDown should be graceful — signal workers to stop after their current task finishes, not mid-task. Track min/max bounds: minimum 1 worker (never scale to zero while dispatcher is running), configurable maximum (default: runtime.NumCPU() or a fixed cap).

IMPORTANT: The existing fixed-worker behavior must be preserved as the default. If no scaling is configured, the pool works exactly as it does today.
acceptance_criteria: Pool supports Resize(target), ScaleUp(n), ScaleDown(n), WorkerCount() methods
Adding workers starts new goroutines reading from the shared task channel
Removing workers is graceful — workers finish current task before exiting
Per-worker quit channels (or equivalent) enable targeted worker shutdown
Minimum worker count enforced (default: 1, configurable)
Maximum worker count enforced (default: runtime.NumCPU(), configurable)
Existing fixed-worker mode works unchanged when scaling is not invoked
Pool metrics (W02) reflect dynamic worker count changes
Shutdown still drains all workers regardless of how many exist
Unit tests cover: scale up, scale down, scale down during active task, min/max bounds, rapid resize
go test -race ./internal/agent/... passes

issues.title: Implement scaling policy engine with configurable thresholds

sections.summary: Create internal/scaling/policy.go that evaluates system and pool metrics and produces scaling decisions (scale up, scale down, hold).
sections.context:
The policy engine is the brain of the auto-scaler. It reads metrics from the system collector and pool, evaluates rules, and returns a decision. It does NOT execute the scaling — that separation keeps the logic testable.

```go
type Decision struct {
    Action     Action    // ScaleUp, ScaleDown, Hold
    Delta      int       // how many workers to add/remove
    Reason     string    // human-readable explanation
    Confidence float64   // 0-1, how sure we are
}

type Action int
const (
    Hold Action = iota
    ScaleUp
    ScaleDown
)

type Policy interface {
    Evaluate(system *metrics.SystemMetrics, pool *agent.PoolMetrics) *Decision
}
```

Default policy (ThresholdPolicy) with configurable YAML:
```yaml
scaling:
  enabled: true
  min_workers: 1
  max_workers: 8
  evaluation_interval: 30s
  cooldown_after_scale: 120s   # don't scale again for 2 minutes
  scale_up:
    cpu_threshold: 60          # scale up if CPU < 60% AND queue has work
    memory_threshold: 80       # don't scale up if memory > 80%
    queue_depth_trigger: 2     # scale up if queue depth >= 2
    all_workers_busy: true     # scale up if all workers active
  scale_down:
    idle_worker_threshold: 2   # scale down if >= 2 workers idle
    idle_duration: 120s        # for at least 2 minutes
    cpu_threshold: 30          # and CPU < 30%
```

Key design principles:
- **Conservative scaling:** Scale up eagerly (queue has work + resources available), scale down slowly (sustained idle period required)
- **Cooldown period:** After any scale event, wait before evaluating again (prevents oscillation)
- **Resource ceiling:** Never scale up if CPU > cpu_threshold or memory > memory_threshold
- **Minimum guarantee:** Never scale below min_workers
- **Confidence scoring:** High confidence when multiple signals agree, low when ambiguous

The policy does NOT know about the pool implementation — it just returns a Decision. The caller (autoscaler loop in W11) applies it.
acceptance_criteria: ThresholdPolicy implements Policy interface
Scale-up decision when: queue has work AND workers are busy AND CPU/memory below ceiling
Scale-down decision when: idle workers above threshold for sustained duration AND CPU is low
Hold decision when: conditions are ambiguous or cooldown is active
Cooldown period prevents rapid oscillation
All thresholds configurable via YAML
Confidence scoring reflects signal agreement
Reason string is human-readable (for logs and dashboard)
Comprehensive unit tests with various metric combinations
Edge cases: zero queue, all idle, all busy, memory pressure, CPU spike
go test -race ./internal/scaling/... passes

issues.title: Verify: Auto-scaling works under simulated load on CT 202

sections.summary: End-to-end validation: enable auto-scaling on CT 202, submit a burst of issues, and verify the pool scales up and then back down.
sections.context:
Deploy the scaling-enabled build to CT 202. Configure with conservative settings (min: 1, max: 5). Create a batch of 6-8 simple task issues on the repo. Observe:

1. Initial state: pool at configured --workers (e.g., 3)
2. Burst submitted: queue fills, all workers busy
3. Autoscaler evaluates: should decide to scale up
4. Workers increase: dashboard shows new worker count
5. Tasks drain: queue empties, workers become idle
6. Autoscaler evaluates: after idle_duration, should scale down
7. Workers decrease: back to baseline

Monitor via:
- Dashboard metrics page (real-time charts)
- journalctl -u samverk-dispatch -f (structured log scaling events)
- MCP get_digest (system health section)

Document results as a timestamped runbook.
acceptance_criteria: Scaling enabled on CT 202 deployment
Pool scales up when burst of tasks fills the queue
Scaling event logged with correct reason and confidence
Dashboard shows worker count change in real-time
Pool scales down after sustained idle period
System remains stable throughout (no crashes, no deadlocks)
CPU and memory stay within configured thresholds during scale-up
Timestamped runbook documenting the full sequence

issues.title: Persist scaling events and metrics history to SQLite

sections.summary: Store scaling events and periodic metric snapshots in SQLite so history survives restarts and enables long-term analysis.
sections.context:
Currently metrics are in-memory rolling windows that reset on restart. For Phase 4 tuning, we need persistent history. Add tables to the existing SQLite store (internal/store/store.go):

```sql
CREATE TABLE scaling_events (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    timestamp TEXT NOT NULL,
    action TEXT NOT NULL,         -- 'scale_up', 'scale_down', 'hold'
    from_workers INTEGER NOT NULL,
    to_workers INTEGER NOT NULL,
    reason TEXT,
    confidence REAL,
    cpu_percent REAL,
    memory_percent REAL,
    queue_depth INTEGER
);

CREATE TABLE metric_snapshots (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    timestamp TEXT NOT NULL,
    cpu_percent REAL,
    memory_percent REAL,
    active_workers INTEGER,
    total_workers INTEGER,
    queue_depth INTEGER,
    avg_task_duration_ms INTEGER,
    goroutine_count INTEGER
);
```

Snapshot interval: every 60 seconds (configurable). Retention: 7 days default, with a cleanup job on startup.

Update /api/v1/metrics/history to read from SQLite when requested duration exceeds in-memory window.

issues.title: Implement task-type duration profiling for smarter routing decisions

sections.summary: Track task duration by agent type and provider, building a profile that the policy engine can use to predict resource needs.
sections.context:
Not all tasks are equal — a code-gen task on claude-opus takes 5-15 minutes, while a triage task on claude-haiku takes 30 seconds. The scaling policy should account for this.

Build a duration profile from historical data:
```go
type TaskProfile struct {
    AgentType       models.AgentType
    Provider        string
    AvgDuration     time.Duration
    P50Duration     time.Duration
    P90Duration     time.Duration
    SampleCount     int
    AvgTokens       int
}
```

Store in SQLite (extend sessions table or create task_profiles table). Update after each task completion. The policy engine (W10) can then predict: 'there are 3 queued code-gen tasks that typically take 8 minutes each — we need more workers to process them within the heartbeat timeout.'

This is a refinement — the policy should work without profiles (fall back to global averages) but make better decisions with them.
acceptance_criteria: Task duration recorded per agent_type + provider combination
Rolling statistics calculated: average, P50, P90, sample count
Profile data persisted to SQLite and survives restarts
Policy engine can optionally use profiles for predictive scaling
Fallback to global averages when insufficient profile data

Unit tests for profile calculation and persistence
